title: terms-priority-annotation-log
content:
Overview / purpose:
This is my personal running log of clause priorities and short talk-tracks for counterparty negotiations where Redwood is the seller (hosted API / dedicated / private). Kept intentionally terse — meant for quick glance before calls and when marking up the PDF redline.

High-level negotiation priorities (ordered):
1) Production continuity (SLOs, fallbacks, transition) — keep service online for customers; limit vendor obligations that create broad, undefined termination triggers.
2) Data treatment & model exposure — protect inputs, outputs, customer embeddings, and avoid language that assigns ownership of derived model weights.
3) Liability and indemnities — cap to committed fees, carve out indirect/third-party limitations, careful with IP indemnity for generated outputs.
4) Confidentiality and auditability — reasonable audit windows, defined scope, minimize on-site or broad data access requirements.
5) Exit / transition assistance — clear export format, timeline, and costs for data egress; avoid vague “reasonable assistance” phrasing.

Quick notes to self (common traps I see):
- Vendors try to slip in language that gives them rights to use anonymized customer data to improve models. Ask for a clear opt-in clause or delete-by-default unless customer consents.
- Watch for "aggregate/derived" language that quietly assigns rights over model improvements (e.g., 'Vendor may use anonymized outputs to improve its models'). Prefer: 'Vendor may not use Customer Data for model training without explicit written consent.'
- Beware of overly broad audit clauses: limit to quarterly, remote unless there's a material incident, and require redaction of other customers' info.
- Don’t accept unlimited termination for convenience tied to vague “material breach” if cure windows are short. Keep cure >= 30 days for complex infra issues.

Suggested clause redlines / talk tracks (short):
- Data usage / training: 
  Seller draft: 'Vendor may use aggregated and anonymized Customer Data to improve services.'
  Counterredline: 'Vendor may not use Customer Data or Outputs for training or improving models unless Customer provides prior written consent. For anonymized or aggregated datasets, Vendor must provide a description of the transformation and retain proof of irreversibility on request.'
  Talk-track: "We run regulated customers — model training on their inputs is a non-starter unless explicitly approved and contractually limited."

- Service levels & remedies: 
  Seller draft: 'Vendor will use commercially reasonable efforts to meet latency targets.'
  Counterredline: 'Vendor commits to the attached SLO table (latency, availability) per route. Credits are the exclusive remedy for SLA failures; liquidated damages capped at X% of monthly fees, not to exceed fees paid in prior 3 months.'
  Talk-track: "We want predictable remedies, not open-ended litigation risk for both sides. Credits align incentives."

- Data residency & export: 
  Seller draft: 'Customer data will be stored in Vendor regions.'
  Counterredline: 'Customer may require data residency limited to (list regions). Upon termination Vendor must provide a full export of Customer Data (including embeddings, KV caches, logs relevant to the account) within 30 days in a structured format (S3-compatible or NDJSON) and certify deletion from all production and backup systems within 90 days.'
  Talk-track: "Export format and timeline are operational — we need specifics so our ops team can plan imports."

- Cache / KV store & backups: 
  Note: If vendor uses shared caching or dedup across customers, flag for potential cross-customer leakage. Ask that caches are partitioned and keys not reused across tenants.

- Telemetry & metrics retention: 
  Ask for clarity: what telemetry does vendor collect (prompt tokens, model id, trace id, full payloads)? Require minimum retention for debugging (30–90 days) but restrict long-term storage unless explicit consent.

- Security incident response:
  Include: notification within 24 hours for confirmed data breaches affecting PII or customer confidentiality; include point of contact, remediation plan, and third-party forensics obligations. Cap forensic costs to reasonable amounts unless breach caused by gross negligence.

- IP / Generated outputs:
  Redline: 'Customer retains all rights to content and outputs generated by Customer inputs.'
  Watch: Vendor may want license to outputs for service improvement — limit to ephemeral debugging access or anonymized metrics only.

- Indemnity buckets to watch:
  - IP infringement (vendor to indemnify for model/weight IP they supply)
  - Data breach & privacy claims (vendor indemnifies for its systems)
  - Third-party content claims (complex when outputs replicate copyrighted materials; carve to 'to the extent caused by Vendor models and not Customer-provided content')
  Suggested cap: fees paid in prior 12 months or a negotiated flat cap; never unlimited unless enterprise-level negotiation with insurance in place.

Open questions to resolve pre-signature (and owners):
- Can Product confirm if embeddings are stored encrypted-at-rest and whether we can request key rotation? (Owner: infra/security)
- Ops: confirm S3/NDJSON export schema for embeddings + prompt history. (Owner: eng-ops)
- Business: what is acceptable SLA credit cap as a % of MRR (Owner: finance)

Negotiation talking tracks / one-liners for calls:
- "We want the product to be safe for regulated customers. Training on customer inputs without explicit consent isn't acceptable. Let's make that carve-out clear."
- "We prefer credits as the predictable remedy for downtime. It's faster and keeps both teams focused on reliability improvements."
- "For export and exit we need machine-readable formats and timestamps. Operational clarity avoids costly disputes later."
- "Audit rights can be remote unless there's a material incident — on-site is expensive and rare, so let's gate it."

Fallback / walkaway metrics (my quick checklist):
- If vendor refuses to put data training ban in writing — escalate to legal; if still refuses, walk away for customers with regulated data.
- If export timeline > 60 days without a concrete operational plan — negotiate or limit use to non-regulated groups.
- If liability cap < 1x annual fees for critical infra — escalate to commercial; consider insurance requirement.

Longer-term items to push for (future contract templates):
- Template addendum for Private deployments detailing on-prem breach response and HSM/KMS integration expectations.
- Standardized export schema for embeddings & prompt logs so our import tooling can be automated.
- Appendix for model-variant fallbacks and compatibility guarantees across releases.

Notes / TODOs: 
- Add a short appendix with concrete NDJSON schema sample (ask eng-ops to draft).
- Confirm whether vendor requires access to raw prompts for model debugging — if yes, require redaction by default and time-limited access with audit trail.

End of scratchpad.

(quick reference: Confluence infra-termination-playbook for our expected export schema; JIRA-7821 = support ticket template we send to vendors for incident response)
